en: Thus have I heard: the Lakkhaṇa Sutta, the thirtieth discourse of the Dīgha Nikāya.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, there are these thirty-two marks of a Great Man possessed by a Great Man, for which there are only two destinations and no other.

If he lives the life of a householder, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch, righteous, a king of Dhamma, conqueror of the four quarters, who has established stability in the land and is endowed with the seven treasures.
These are his seven treasures, namely:
the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh.
He has more than a thousand sons who are brave, heroic, well-built, and crushers of enemy armies.
Having conquered this earth bounded by the ocean without punishment or sword, he dwells there through righteousness.
But if he goes forth from the home life into homelessness, he becomes an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha, who draws back the veil from the world.
And what, monks, are those thirty-two marks of a Great Man possessed by which a Great Man has only two possible destinies and no other?
If he dwells at home, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch...
[as before] ...but if he goes forth from the home life into homelessness, he becomes an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One who draws back the veil from the world.
"Here, monks, a Great Man has well-planted feet. That, monks, is a mark of a Great Man that this Great Man possesses.
Furthermore, monks, on the soles of the Great Man's feet, wheels have appeared with a thousand spokes, complete with rims and hubs, perfect in every aspect. That, monks, is a mark of a Great Man..."
His feet have wheels with a thousand spokes, complete with rims and hubs, perfect in every aspect;
this too, monks, is a mark of a Great Man.
Furthermore, monks, a Great Man has long heels... [and so on].
He has long fingers;
he has soft and tender hands and feet;
he has webbed hands and feet.
He has ankles that do not protrude;
he has calves like those of an antelope;
standing without bending, he can touch and rub both knees with the palms of his hands.
He has the male organ concealed in a sheath;
he is golden-colored, with skin like refined gold;
he has delicate skin, and because his skin is so delicate, dust and dirt do not adhere to his body.
He has a single hair to each pore; the hairs grow one by one from each pore.
He has upward-pointing body hairs; the hairs grow pointing upwards, blue-black in color like collyrium, curled like rings, and turning to the right.
He has a body straight like that of Brahmā.
He has a body that is well-proportioned; he has the forequarters of a lion;
he has a rounded torso.
He is well-proportioned like a banyan tree: as long as his body is, so long is his span [from hand to hand], and as long as his span is, so long is his body;
he has symmetrical shoulders;
he has the finest sense of taste.
He has a jaw like a lion’s;
he has forty teeth;
his teeth are even.
He has teeth that are closely set;
he has very white teeth;
he has a large tongue.
He has the voice of Brahmā, speaking with the sound of a cuckoo;
he has deep blue eyes;
and he has eyelashes like those of a cow.
A tuft of hair grows between his eyebrows, white and soft like cotton wool. Monks,
that a Great Man has a tuft of hair growing between his eyebrows, white and soft like cotton wool—
this too, monks, is a mark of a Great Man.
Furthermore, monks, a Great Man has a head like a turban. That a Great Man has a head like a turban, monks, is also a mark of a Great Man.
These, monks, are those thirty-two marks of a Great Man, endowed with which a Great Man has only two possible destinies and no other:

if he lives the life of a householder, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch... [as before] ...if he goes forth from the household life into homelessness, he becomes a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One.
But if he goes forth from the home life into homelessness, he becomes an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One who has removed the veil from the world.
These, monks, are the thirty-two marks of a Great Man that even outside ascetics bear; yet they do not know:
"By the performance of this deed, this mark is acquired."
1. The Mark of Well-Placed Feet:

Furthermore, monks, in his former births, former existences, and former abodes, when he was formerly a human being, the Tathāgata was firm in his undertaking of wholesome states and steadfast in his undertaking of good conduct of body and good conduct of speech.
In regard to good mental conduct— namely, generosity and sharing, undertaking moral discipline, observing the Uposatha fast, filiality toward one's mother, filiality toward one's father,
respect for recluses, respect for brahmins, honoring those who are senior in the family, and various other superior wholesome qualities— he, because of having performed,
accumulated, increased, and expanded that karma, upon the breakup of the body after death, is reborn in a happy destination, a heavenly world.
Thus, there he surpasses other devas in ten respects: by divine life-span, by divine beauty,
by divine happiness, by divine fame, by divine sovereignty, and by divine forms,
sounds, odors, tastes, and tactile objects.
Having passed away from there and returned to this state of existence, he acquires this mark of a Great Man:
his feet are well-placed.
He sets his foot down evenly upon the ground, lifts it up evenly, and touches the earth with the entire surface of both soles evenly.

Endowed with that mark, if he lives the life of a householder, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch, righteous, a king of Dharma, conqueror of the four quarters, stabilizer of the land, and possessor of the seven treasures.
These are his seven treasures:
namely, the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh.
Furthermore, he has more than a thousand sons who are brave, heroic in form, and crushers of enemy armies.

Having conquered this earth, bounded by the ocean—free from barrenness, free from marks of distress, free from thorns, prosperous, flourishing, secure, auspicious, and free from affliction—he dwells there, ruling by Dhamma, without the rod and without the sword.
Being a king, what does he obtain?
He is unshakable by any human adversary or enemy.
If he remains a king, he gains this;
but if he goes forth from the home life into homelessness, he becomes an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One who has removed the veil from the world.
Being enlightened, what does one obtain?
One becomes unshakable by internal or external adversaries, by enemies or foes, by passion, hatred, or delusion, or by any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world.
Being enlightened, one obtains this.
The Blessed One spoke this matter.
Regarding this, it is said:
"In truth, in the Dhamma, in self-taming, and in self-restraint,"
He delighted in purity, virtuous conduct, and the observance of the Uposatha; he was devoted to giving, non-violence, and the absence of cruelty,
having firmly undertaken and practiced them in their entirety.
Thus, by that kamma, he ascended to heaven and experienced happiness and the delights of play; then,
passing away from there, he has returned here once more.
He touched the earth with both feet.
The assembled experts in physiognomy declared:
"For one who stands with such even footing, there is no need for support."
Whether for a householder or one who has gone forth,
that characteristic exists as an indicator of that purpose.
One who dwells at home becomes unshakable.
Unconquered by enemies and not to be crushed by anyone while existing here as a human being—
such is one through the fruit of that kamma.
But if such a person goes forth,
one who delights in the desire for renunciation and possesses clear vision,
he never at any time becomes a stumbling block.
"For this is the nature of that Supreme Man.
2. The Mark of the Wheel on the Soles of the Feet:
"Monks, in whatever former birth, former existence, former abode, when the Tathāgata was formerly a human being,"
He brought happiness to many people, dispelled their agitation, terror, and fear, and provided righteous protection, defense, and security; he also gave gifts along with their retinues.
Because of having performed, accumulated, increased, and expanded that karma, upon the breakup of the body after death, he was reborn in a happy destination, a heavenly world...
[passage omitted] ...having passed away from there and returned to this state of existence, he acquires this mark of a Great Man.
On the soles of his feet, wheels have appeared, with a thousand spokes, complete with rims and hubs, perfect in every aspect, and well-proportioned in their intervals.
Endowed with this mark, if he lives the life of a householder, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch...
What does he obtain when he is a king?
He has a great retinue;

his retinue consists of many brahmins and householders, town-dwellers and country-folk, accountants and high officials, military officers, gatekeepers, ministers, counselors, kings, feudal lords, and princes.
Being a king, he receives this.
But if he goes forth from the home life into homelessness, he becomes an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One who has removed the veil from the world.
Being a Buddha, what does he obtain?
He has a great retinue.
"He has a great retinue: monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, gods, humans, asuras, nāgas, and gandhabbas.
Being a Buddha, he obtains this.
This is the meaning the Blessed One spoke.
Regarding this, it is said:
“In former times, in previous births,
having become a human being, he brought happiness to many.”
Dispelling the fear of anxiety and terror,
and eager for protections and safeguards,
he ascended to heaven by means of that deed.
He enjoyed happiness and the delights of play;
then, passing away from there,
he has returned here again and finds wheels upon his two feet.
Having seen the prince, who possessed the marks of a hundred merits, the assembled fortune-tellers prophesied a thousandfold destinies for him.
He will have a retinue and be a crusher of his enemies.
For such a one as this, with wheels possessing naves on all sides,
would not [otherwise] enter the homeless life.
He turns the wheel and rules the earth;
behind him follow the kshatriyas,
who surround him of great renown.
But if such a wise one, delighting in the aspiration for renunciation, enters the homeless life,
then gods, humans, asuras, sakkas, and rakkhasas [will honor him].
Gandhabbas, nāgas, birds, and quadrupeds surround him who is unsurpassed, honored by gods and humans,
and possessed of great fame.
3–5. The Characteristic of Long and Shaped Fingers:
"Bhikkhus, in whatever former birth, former existence, or former abode, when the Tathāgata was formerly a human being, he abandoned the taking of life and abstained from taking life;
he laid aside the rod and the weapon, and dwelt modest, compassionate, and full of sympathy, concerned for the welfare and well-being of all living beings."
Thus, because that karma was performed, accumulated, intensified, and expanded...
[as before] ...having passed away from there and come to this state of existence, he acquires these three marks of a Great Man:
he has long heels, long fingers, and a body as straight as Brahmā’s.
Endowed with those marks, if he lives the life of a householder, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch...
What does he obtain when he is a king?
He is long-lived and long-enduring; he maintains a long lifespan, and it is impossible for any human enemy or adversary to take his life prematurely.
Being a king, one obtains this... [as before] ...
Being a Buddha, what does one obtain?
One becomes long-lived and long-enduring; one maintains a long life-span, and it is not possible for one's life to be cut short prematurely.
“Being a Buddha, he gains this: that he is not opposed by adversaries or enemies— whether by a recluse, a brahmin, a deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world.”
The Blessed One spoke this matter.
Regarding this, it is said:
“Having understood for oneself the fear of death and slaughter, ...”
He abstained from killing others;
by that well-performed conduct he went to heaven and experienced the ripening fruit of his good deeds.
But having returned here again as a Caviya,
he acquires three characteristics here:
he becomes one with broad, long, and smooth heels.
Brahmā indeed is straight, beautiful, and well-born of limb.
He has beautiful arms, is well-nourished, well-proportioned, and well-born;
his fingers are soft and tender.
By three marks of a supreme man,
they indicate that the prince will live long;
if he remains a householder, he will live for a long time.
If one goes forth for a very long time and thereby sustains oneself through the development of the bases of psychic power, this is the sign of long life.
6. The Characteristic of Being Dear to Beings:

"Furthermore, monks, in a former birth, in a former existence, in a former abode, when he was formerly a human being, the Tathāgata was a giver of choice, flavorful foods—both solid and soft, those to be chewed, swallowed, tasted, licked, and drunk."
Thus, because of having performed that deed...
[as before] ...having passed away from there and come to this state of existence, he acquires this mark of a Great Man: he is well-proportioned, possessing seven protuberances;
there are protuberances on both hands, protuberances on both feet, protuberances on both shoulders, and there is a protuberance on the back of the neck.
Endowed with that mark, if he lives the life of a householder, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch...
What does he obtain when he is a king?
He obtains exquisite, delicious foods—solid foods, soft foods, foods to be sucked, foods to be licked, and drinks.
Being a king, he gains this...
[as before] ...being a Buddha, what does he gain?
He is a recipient of exquisite, flavorful foods—hard foods, soft foods, foods to be sucked, foods to be licked, and drinks.
“Being a Buddha, one obtains this.
The Blessed One spoke this matter.
Regarding this, it is said:
“He was a giver of the finest flavors of food to be chewed, eaten, licked, and drunk;
by that well-performed deed, he— ”
He rejoices for a long time in the Nandana grove.
He attains here the seven softnesses and finds pliancy of hand and foot.
Those skilled in the signs of terminology say that this [term] is for the sake of obtaining various kinds of food and drink;
for even among householders, it serves to indicate that same purpose.
And he attains even the going-forth,
which is the supreme gain of edible and drinkable food and flavors;
they call it the severing of all household bonds.
7–8. The Characteristics of Soft, Webbed Hands and Feet:
“Monks, in whatever former birth, former existence, and former abode, when the Tathāgata was formerly a human being, he was one who gathered people together by means of the four bases of sympathy.”
By means of generosity, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality.
Because he performed that action...
[as before] ...having passed away from there and come to this state of existence, he acquires these two marks of a Great Man.
He has soft hands and feet, and his hands and feet have webbed fingers and toes.
Endowed with these marks, if he lives the life of a householder, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch...
[as before] ...being such a king, what does he obtain?

He has his retinue well-gathered; his brahmins and householders, town-dwellers and country-folk, accountants and high officials, military officers, gatekeepers, ministers, counselors, other kings, revenue-collectors, and princes are well-gathered.
Being a king, he gains this...
being a Buddha, what does he gain?
“He has his retinue well-gathered; his bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, male lay followers, female lay followers, devas, humans, asuras, nāgas, and gandhabbas are well-gathered.
Being a Buddha, he gains this. Thus the Blessed One spoke.
Regarding this, it is said:
“Generosity, conduct for the welfare of others,
affectionate speech, and impartiality;”
By well-comprising the practice of duties for many,
one goes to heaven through irreproachable virtue.
Having passed away and returned here once again, [one attains the goal].
The youth, tender and delicate, acquires softness in his hands and feet, webbed fingers, and an exceedingly radiant, charming, and beautiful appearance.
He becomes one whose retinue is obedient and compliant,
dwelling in greatness and well-restrained; speaking kindly,
he seeks to bring about their welfare and happiness.
He practices the qualities that he has taken to heart.
And if he should renounce all sensual enjoyments,
the Victor speaks a discourse on the Dhamma to the people.
“Having gained deep confidence in one who corrects his speech, they listen and practice in accordance with the Dhamma. 9–10.
The characteristics of the upturned feet and the upward-pointing body hair on the soles.

“Bhikkhus, when the Tathāgata—in a former birth, a former existence, a former abode—being then a human being, spoke words conducive to welfare and conducive to the Dhamma, instructing many people, bringing benefit and happiness to living beings, and being a donor of the Dhamma;
by having performed that action... [and so on].”
Passing away from there and returning to this state of existence, he acquires these two marks of a Great Man:
his heels are prominent, and the hair on his body grows upward.
Endowed with these marks, if he lives the life of a householder, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch... [and so forth].
Being a king, what does he obtain?
He becomes the foremost, the best, the leader, the highest, and the most excellent among those who enjoy sensual pleasures.
Being a king, he obtains this... [and so on].
Having become a Buddha, what does one obtain?
One becomes the foremost, the best, the leader, the supreme, and the most excellent among all beings.
Having become a Buddha, one obtains this.
The Blessed One spoke this matter.
Regarding this, it is said:
“In former times, his speech was endowed with meaning and the Dhamma;”
He showed this path to many people;
bringing welfare and happiness to living beings,
he lived by means of the sacrifice of the Dharma and was free from stinginess.
By that well-performed action,
he goes to a happy destination and rejoices there;
having returned here, he possesses two marks.
He attains preeminence among the best.
With the hair on his body standing erect like a hare,
the ankle-bones of his feet are beautifully positioned.
Covered with flesh and blood, bound by skin,
and beautiful only when standing upright—
if such a person were to dwell in a house, [what would he do?]
He goes to the foremost rank among those who enjoy sensual pleasures;
no one is found superior to him,
for he moves having overcome the whole of Jambudīpa.
And even after going forth, he of unsurpassed exertion attains the highest state among all living beings;
therefore, no one is found superior to him.
“He dwells having overcome the entire world.
11. The Mark of the Antelope-Legs:
“Monks, in whatever former birth, former existence, former abode, when the Tathāgata was formerly a human being...”
He was one who taught respectfully—whether it was a craft, a science, a conduct, or a work—thinking:
“How might they understand quickly, practice quickly, and not suffer for long?
Because he had performed that deed... [and so on].
Having passed away from there and returned to this state of existence, he acquires this mark of a Great Man:
his shanks are like those of an antelope.
Endowed with this mark, if he lives the life of a householder, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch... [and so forth].
Being a king, what does he obtain?
He quickly obtains those things that are worthy of a king, the attributes of a king, the enjoyments of a king, and what is befitting for a king.
Being a king, this is what he obtains... [and so on].
Being a Buddha, what does one obtain?
One quickly obtains those things that are worthy of a recluse, the requisites of a recluse, the enjoyments of a recluse, and what is appropriate for a recluse.
Being a Buddha, one obtains this.
The Blessed One spoke this matter.
Regarding this, it is said:
“In crafts, in the sciences and conduct, and in works...”
He desires that they may understand quickly:
what does not lead to the harm of anyone,
he recites swiftly and does not weary for long.
Having performed that wholesome deed which brings about happiness as its fruit,
one obtains beautiful and well-proportioned shanks—
rounded, well-formed, and tapering like a mung bean.
With hair standing upright and skin so delicate it seems to rise from it—
such a person is called "one with shanks like an antelope's.
This is said to be a mark here that brings about swift success.
When one desires things that are in accordance with the household life,
even without having gone forth, one quickly attains them here;
and if such a person does go forth, [they attain even more].
Delighting in the desire for renunciation,
the discerning one quickly attains that which is appropriate and conformable to his state, through the movement of his mind.
12. The Mark of Fine Skin:
"Monks, in whatever former birth, former existence, and former abode, when the Tathāgata was formerly a human being, he would approach a recluse or a brahmin and inquire: [as follows]"
‘Venerable sir, what is wholesome? What is unwholesome? What is blameworthy? What is blameless? What should be cultivated?
What should not be cultivated? And what, being done by me, would lead to my harm and suffering for a long time;
or what, being done by me, would lead to my welfare and happiness for a long time?’”
Thus, because he performed that deed...
[as before] ...having passed away from there and come to this state of existence, he acquires this mark of a Great Man:
his skin is fine; because his skin is fine, dust and dirt do not adhere to his body.
Endowed with that mark, if he lives the life of a householder, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch...
[as before] ...being a king, what does he obtain?
He possesses great wisdom; among those who enjoy sensual pleasures, there is no one equal or superior to him in wisdom.
Being a king, he gains this...
[and so on] ...being a Buddha, what does he gain?
He possesses great wisdom, vast wisdom, radiant wisdom, swift wisdom, sharp wisdom, and penetrative wisdom; among all beings, there is no one equal or superior to him in wisdom.
“Being a Buddha, one obtains this.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Regarding this, it is said:
“Pure, in former births,
he was desirous of knowledge and was one who asked questions thoroughly;
he was eager to learn and attended upon those gone forth.”
Another person listened to the commentary.
By the deed of attaining wisdom,
having become a human being, he possessed delicate skin.
Those skilled in the signs of portents have declared:
"He will perceive subtle matters through direct insight.
If such a person does not go forth into the homeless life,"
He turns the wheel and rules the earth;
in matters of instruction and in his possessions,
no one is found who is better or even equal to him.
But if such a person as this goes forth into homelessness,
delighting in the aspiration for renunciation and being discerning,
he attains the unsurpassed excellence of wisdom.
“The one of excellent and vast intelligence attains enlightenment.
13. The Mark of Golden Color:
“Monks, in whatever former birth, former existence, and former abode, when the Tathāgata was formerly a human being...”
He was free from anger and largely devoid of distress;
even when spoken to much, he did not become resentful, did not grow angry, did not harbor ill will, and did not remain obstinate; he manifested neither anger, nor hatred, nor resentment.
And he was a giver of fine, soft rugs and coverlets—of exquisite linen, exquisite cotton, exquisite silk, and exquisite wool.
Thus, because that deed was performed and accumulated...
[and so on] ...having passed away from there and come to this state of existence, he acquires this mark of a Great Man:
he is golden-hued, with skin like refined gold.
Endowed with that mark, if he dwells in the household life, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch...
What does he obtain when he is a king?
He obtains fine, soft rugs and coverlets; fine linen, fine cotton, fine silk, and fine wool.
Being a king, he obtains this...
[as before] ...Being a Buddha, what does he obtain?
He is a recipient of fine, soft spreads and coverlets: fine linen, fine cotton, fine silk, and fine wool.
“Being a Buddha, one obtains this.
Thus the Blessed One spoke.
Regarding this, it is said:
“He resolved upon non-anger and gave gifts—
fine garments of exquisite texture;
while dwelling in a previous existence, he bestowed them abundantly.”
Like a rain-god showering down great abundance,
having performed that deed, when he passed away from here,
he was reborn in the divine realm, experiencing the ripening of the fruit of his well-done deeds.
One who resembles a body of gold prevails here,
like the moon from the most excellent tree of the gods;
such a person dwells at home and does not go forth.
He rules over the great earth with righteousness; having subdued it here,
he obtains a stainless, delicate skin and purity.
If one who has obtained coverings, robes,
and outer garments enters the homeless life,
being disciplined, he experiences the fruit of what was done previously.
“There is no loss of what has been done.
14. The mark of the male organ being concealed in a sheath:
“Monks, in whatever former birth, former existence, former abode, when the Tathāgata was formerly a human being...”
He was one who reunited kinsmen, friends, dear ones,

and companions who had long been lost or had lived abroad for a very long time. He reunited mothers with their sons, sons with their mothers, fathers with their sons, sons with their fathers, and brothers with their brothers.
He brought together a brother with a sister, he brought together a sister with a brother, and he brought together a sister with a sister; having united them, he rejoiced in it.
Because of having performed that deed... [pe]...
Passing away from there and returning to this state of existence, he acquires this mark of a Great Man:
his private parts are enclosed in a sheath.
Endowed with this mark, if he lives the life of a householder, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch... [and so forth]...
Being a king, what does he obtain?
He has many sons; indeed, he may have more than a thousand sons who are brave, heroic, well-built, and capable of crushing enemy armies.
Being a king, he obtains this... [and so forth].
What does one obtain upon becoming a Buddha?
One has many sons; indeed, one’s sons number in the thousands, being brave, heroic in form, and crushers of enemy armies.
This is what one obtains upon becoming a Buddha.
The Blessed One spoke this matter.
Regarding this, it is said:
“In former times, in previous births, in the cities of the past...”
He gathered together his kinsmen, dear friends, and companions who had long been lost and had lived abroad for a very long time;
having reunited them, he expressed his gratitude.
Thus, by that karma, he ascended to heaven and experienced happiness and the delights of play; then,
passing away from there, he has returned here once more.
He finds a wife who covers his body with her garment.
Such a man becomes one who has many sons;
indeed, more than a thousand children may be born to him.
Brave, heroic, and scorers of their enemies,
speaking kindly and generating joy in the householder—
these are far more numerous for one who lives the life of a renunciant.
Sons follow the words of their parents,
whether they be householders or those who have gone forth;
that characteristic arises as a signifier of that purpose.
The first recitation section is finished.
15–16. The characteristics of being well-rounded, not stooping, and reaching down to the knees:
"Monks, when the Tathāgata, in a former birth, a former existence, a former abode, having previously been a human being..."
Considering how to gather the great multitude of people, he knew rightly and knew for himself; he knew the person and knew the distinction between persons:
“This one is worthy of this; that one is worthy of that. Thus, in various instances, he was a maker of distinctions among persons. Because of having performed that deed... [and so on].
Passing away from there and returning to this state of existence, he acquires these two marks of a Great Man:
his body is as well-proportioned as a banyan tree; and while standing upright without bending, he can touch and rub both palms against his knees.

Endowed with these marks, if he lives the life of a householder, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch... [as before] ...if he goes forth from the household life into homelessness, he becomes a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One.
What does one gain by being a king?
One becomes wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments; one has abundant gold and silver, abundant assets and requisites, abundant wealth and grain, with full treasuries and storehouses.
By being a king, one gains this... [and so forth].
When one is a Buddha, what does one obtain?
One becomes wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments.
These are his riches, namely:
“The wealth of faith, the wealth of virtue, the wealth of moral shame, the wealth of moral dread, the wealth of learning, the wealth of generosity, and the wealth of wisdom—
being a Buddha, one obtains these.
Thus the Blessed One spoke this matter.
Regarding this, it is said:
“Having weighed, investigated, and reflected,
while considering how to gather the great masses of people;”
This man, who was once a maker of distinctions among men, was worthy here and there;
yet, standing upon the earth, he did not bend down.
With both hands she touched her knees;
she became as perfectly rounded as a tree trunk by the remaining fruit of her well-performed deeds.
Skilled in the knowledge of many various omens and marks,
extremely subtle men made their predictions;
they spoke of many various things that were worthy for householders.
A young, tender boy obtains [it]. And here,
there are many who enjoy sensual pleasures under the lord of the earth,
appearing in the form of householders.
"And if one renounces all sensual enjoyments, one obtains the unsurpassed, supreme, and highest treasure. 17–19.
The Three Marks beginning with the Forepart of the Body Being Like That of a Lion.
“Monks, in whatever former birth, former existence, and former abode, when I was formerly a human being,
I desired the welfare of many people, their benefit, their well-being, and their security from bondage, [thinking]:
‘How might they increase in faith, increase in virtue, increase in learning, and increase in generosity?’”
‘May they increase in accordance with the Dhamma; may they increase in wisdom; may they increase in wealth and grain;
may they increase in fields and lands; may they increase in bipeds and quadrupeds; may they increase in wives and children; may they increase in slaves, laborers, and servants;
may they increase in kinsmen; may they increase in friends; may they increase in relatives.’”
Thus, by having performed that karma...
[as before] ...having passed away from there and come to this state of existence, he acquires these three marks of a Great Man:
his torso is like that of a lion, his chest is broad, and his shoulders are perfectly rounded.
Endowed with these marks, if he lives the life of a householder, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch...
What does he obtain as a king?

He is of a nature not subject to decline; he does not fall away from wealth and grain, fields and lands, bipeds and quadrupeds, children and wives, slaves, laborers, and servants, kinsmen, friends, and relatives; he does not fall away from all his prosperity.
Being a king, he obtains this...
[and so on] ...being a Buddha, what does he obtain?
He is of a nature not subject to decline; he does not fall away from faith, virtue, learning, generosity, or wisdom; he does not fall away from any excellence whatsoever.
“Being a Buddha, one obtains this.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Regarding this, it is said:
“By faith, virtue, learning, and wisdom;
by generosity, righteousness, and many good deeds;
by wealth, grain, and fields and lands—”
With children, wives, and quadrupeds;
with kinsmen, friends, and relatives;
with strength, beauty, and happiness—both kinds.
He desired that they should not decline,
yet he longed for sleep regarding his welfare;
thus he became well-proportioned like the forequarters of a lion.
With shoulders well-rounded and a chest broad between them,
that was his sign of excellence, produced by deeds well-performed in the past and never diminished.
The householder prospers through grain and wealth,
through sons, wives, and quadrupeds;
but the renunciant, possessing nothing, attains the unsurpassed.
“He attains enlightenment through the quality of being incapable of being defeated.
“Monks, that the Tathāgata, in a former birth, a former existence, a former abode, having previously been a human being, [possessed] the mark of having a tongue reaching to the top of his head...”
He was by nature non-violent toward living beings, whether with his hand, a clod of earth, a staff, or a weapon.
Because he performed and accumulated that karma...

[as before] ...having passed away from there and come to this state of existence, he acquires this mark of a Great Man: he has an exquisite sense of taste; the taste-carrying channels in his neck are developed upward and convey flavors evenly.
Endowed with that mark, if he lives the life of a householder, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch...
What does he obtain when he is a king?
He is free from illness and free from affliction; he possesses a digestive faculty that is well-balanced, being neither too cold nor too hot.
Being a king, he obtains this...
[and so on] ...being a Buddha, what does he obtain?
He is free from illness and free from affliction; he possesses a digestive faculty that is well-balanced, being neither too cold nor too hot, but moderate and fit for striving.
“Being a Buddha, one obtains this.
The Blessed One spoke this matter.
Regarding this, it is said:
“Nor indeed by blows with the hands, nor with a clod,
nor with a weapon, nor by execution or death;
nor by oppression or by reviling.”
He did not harm the people below, for he was one who harms none.
Because of that, having attained a happy destination, he rejoices;
having performed deeds with happy fruit, he experiences happiness.
The taste-carrying channel is well-established and symmetrical;
one who has come here obtains the supreme excellence of flavors.
Therefore, those who are exceedingly skillful and discerning call him by that name.
"This person will be full of happiness;
whether as a householder or again as one gone forth,
that mark exists as an indicator of that benefit."
21–22. The Characteristics of Deep Blue Eyes and Eyelashes like those of a Cow:

“Monks, in whatever former birth, former existence, and former abode, when the Tathāgata was formerly a human being, he did not look with a scattered gaze, nor with a wandering gaze, nor looking about this way and that;
rather, with an upright mind, straight and even, he looked upon many people with eyes of affection.
Because he performed that deed...
[as before] ...having passed away from there and come to this state of existence, he acquires these two marks of a Great Man:
his eyes are deep blue and his eyelashes are like those of a cow.
Endowed with these marks, if he lives the life of a householder, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch...
What does he obtain when he is a king?
He is lovely to behold to many people; he is dear and pleasing to brahmins and householders, and to those of the towns and the countryside.
Of the chief accountants, the army officers, the gatekeepers, the ministers, the councilors, the rulers, the provincial governors, and the princes.
Being a king, he receives these...
[as before] ...Being a Buddha, what does he receive?
“He becomes pleasing to many people; he is beloved and agreeable to monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, devas, humans, asuras, nāgas, and gandhabbas.
Being a Buddha, he obtains this. Thus the Blessed One spoke.
Concerning this, it is said:
Neither straying nor wandering,
nor yet looking about with deliberation;
Straightforward, as well as upright in mind,
he gazed upon many people with a friendly eye.
He [experiences] the ripening of the fruit in happy destinies.
There he experiences and rejoices; and here,
moreover, he becomes one with cow-like eyes,
with deep blue eyes and a handsome appearance.
Diligent and skillful, many men are experts in signs;
they are adept at perceiving even the most subtle details.
They designate him as "Piyadassana" (the one of lovely appearance).
Being of lovely appearance, whether a householder or one who has gone forth,
he becomes beloved by many people.
And if he does not become a monk, he remains a householder;
beloved by many, he is the destroyer of sorrow.
23. The mark of the turbaned head.
“Furthermore, monks, in a former birth, a former existence, a former abode, when the Tathāgata was formerly a human being, he was a leader of many people in wholesome states;
he was a guide for many people in good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind,
in the sharing of gifts, in the undertaking of virtue, in the observance of the Uposatha, and in filial piety toward mother and father.”
Through his practice of the state of a recluse, the state of a brahmin, reverence for elders in the family, and various other superior wholesome qualities;
by having performed that karma...
[as before] ...having passed away from there and come to this state of existence, he acquires this mark of a Great Man:
He has a turban-shaped head.
Endowed with this mark, if he lives the life of a householder, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch...
[as before] ...being such a king, what does he obtain?

A great multitude follows him: brahmins and householders, town-dwellers and country-folk, accountants and high officials, military officers, gatekeepers, ministers, counselors, kings, feudal lords, and princes.
Being a king, he receives these things...
[as before] ...being a Buddha, what does he receive?
“A great multitude follows him: monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, gods, humans, asuras, nāgas, and gandhabbas.
Being a Buddha, he gains this. Thus the Blessed One spoke.
Regarding this, it is said:
“He was a leader in good deeds,
delighting in the practice of Dhamma among all things.”
He became a benefactor to many people and experienced the fruit of his merit in the heavenly realms.
Having experienced that fruit of his well-conducted life, he...
He has attained the mark of the turbaned head;
those who bear the signs of physiognomy have declared:
"He will be a leader for many people."
Then, even before that, people here bring him enjoyments;
if he becomes a khattiya, a lord of the earth.
He gains favor among the many people.
And if that person goes forth into homelessness,
he becomes proficient in the teachings and wise.
“The great multitude becomes his follower,
delighting in the virtues of his instruction.
(24–25) The characteristics of having a single hair per pore and being warm.
“Furthermore, monks, in a former birth, a former existence, a former abode, when I was formerly a human being, I abandoned false speech and abstained from false speech;
I was a speaker of truth, devoted to truth, trustworthy, reliable, and not a deceiver of the world.
By having performed and accumulated that kamma... [pe]...”
Having passed away from there and returned to this state of existence, he acquires these two marks of a Great Man:
his body hairs grow one to each pore, and between his eyebrows grows a tuft of hair that is white, soft like cotton-wool.

Endowed with these marks, if he lives the life of a householder, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch... [as before] ...if he goes forth from the household life into homelessness, he becomes a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One.
Being a king, what does he obtain?

A great multitude attends upon him: brahmins and householders, town-dwellers and country-folk, accountants, high officials, military officers, gatekeepers, ministers, counselors, other kings, landowners, and princes.
Being a king, he obtains this... [and so forth].
Being a Buddha, what does one obtain?
A great multitude of people attend upon him: monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, gods, humans, asuras, nāgas, and gandhabbas.
Being a Buddha, one obtains this.
The Blessed One spoke this matter.
Regarding this, it is said:
“True to his promise in former births,”
Speaking without duplicity, he avoided falsehood;
he was never one to deceive anyone,
speaking only what is real, true, and such as it is.
His hair between the eyebrows was white, exceedingly bright, and soft like cotton; it was well-formed,
and no two hairs grew from a single pore.
He had limbs covered with hair growing from each single pore.
Many experts in marks, skilled in discerning the signs of future arising, assembled and made a prediction concerning him.
Just as the tuft of hair and the body hairs are well-arranged,
so too does the multitude of people follow after such a one;
even when he is a householder, the people follow after him.
“By virtue of much karma performed in the past,
people continue to follow even one who has gone forth as a homeless ascetic, who is without possessions, unsurpassed, and is a Buddha.”
26–27. The Forty Teeth with Gaps as a Mark:

“Monks, in whatever former birth, former existence, or former abode, when the Tathāgata was formerly a human being, he abandoned malicious speech and abstained from malicious speech. Having heard something here, he did not report it there...”
Having heard something here, he did not repeat it elsewhere to divide those people from these; nor, having heard something there, did he repeat it here to divide these people from those.

Thus, he was a reconciler of those who were divided and a promoter of harmony among those who were united. He delighted in concord, rejoiced in concord, found joy in concord, and spoke words that bring about concord.
Thus, by having performed that deed ... [and so on] ...
passing away from there and coming to this state of existence, he acquires these two marks of a Great Man:
he has forty teeth, and his teeth are without gaps.
Endowed with those marks, if he lives the life of a householder, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch...
What does he obtain when he is a king?

He has an invincible assembly; his assembly is invincible: brahmins, householders, town-dwellers and country-folk, accountants and high officials, military officers, gatekeepers, ministers, counselors, vassal kings, treasurers, and princes.
Being a king, he gains this...
Being a Buddha, what does he gain?
He has an indivisible assembly; his assembly is indivisible: monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, gods, humans, asuras, nāgas, and gandhabbas.
“Being a Buddha, one obtains this.
Thus the Blessed One spoke.
Regarding this, it is said:
“One who causes division among those in harmony,
who incites disputes that increase dissension,
and who performs improper acts that increase quarreling— ”
He did not speak words that cause division among those who are united;
he spoke sweet speech that increases harmony and brings about reconciliation among those who are divided.
He who is endowed with these qualities dispels strife among people;
he rejoices and delights in harmony.
He will experience the ripening of the fruit in the happy realms.
There he experiences [pleasure] and rejoices;
here his teeth are tamed, not gapped, closely set,
four in each row, and well-formed.
If he becomes a Khattiya, a lord of the earth,
his assembly will be indivisible;
and he becomes a recluse, free from passion and stainless.
“The assembly follows him and remains steadfast.
28–29. Regarding the characteristics of having a broad tongue and a Brahma-like voice:
“Monks, in whatever former birth, former existence, former abode, and in whatever previous life as a human being the Tathāgata was, [he possessed these qualities].”

Having abandoned harsh speech, he abstained from harsh speech. He became one who speaks such words as are gentle, pleasing to the ear, endearing, heart-stirring, urbane, agreeable to many people, and dear to many people.
By having performed and accumulated that action...
[as before] ...having passed away from there and come to this state of existence, he acquires these two marks of a Great Man.
He has a broad tongue and a Brahma-voice, speaking with the voice of a cuckoo.
Endowed with these marks, if he lives the life of a householder, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch...
What does he obtain when he is a king?

He is one whose speech is authoritative; his words are accepted by brahmins and householders, by those in towns and countryside, by accountants and high officials, by military officers, gatekeepers, ministers, councilors, kings, landowners, and princes.
Being a king, he gains this...
[and so on] ...being a Buddha, what does he gain?
“He has speech that is worthy of being accepted; his words are heeded by monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, gods, humans, asuras, nāgas, and gandhabbas.
Being a Buddha, he obtains this.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Regarding this, it is said:
“[One who] acts with abuse, quarreling,
and harassment, who is oppressive and crushes many people;”
He did not utter harsh or violent speech;
he spoke words that were sweet, well-composed, and gentle.
They were pleasing to the mind and went straight to the heart.
He utters speech that is pleasant to the ear;
he experiences the fruit of well-spoken words—
experience the fruit of merit in the heavenly realms.
Having understood the fruit of well-conducted conduct,
he attained this Brahma-like voice; his tongue is vast and broad.
He speaks words that are worthy of being accepted.
Even for a householder, it succeeds just as he says;
and if that man goes forth into homelessness, it likewise succeeds.
The people heeded his word as he spoke much that was well-spoken, though it was already much. 30.
The Lion-Jaw Characteristic.

“Furthermore, monks, in a former birth, a former existence, a former dwelling, when I was formerly a human being, having abandoned idle chatter, I abstained from idle chatter; I spoke at the proper time, spoke truthfully, spoke meaningfully, spoke on the Dhamma, spoke on the Vinaya;
I was one who spoke words that were worth treasuring—timely, accompanied by reasons, measured, and connected with the goal.”
Because he performed that deed ...
[as before] ... having passed away from there and come to this state of existence, he acquires this mark of a Great Man:
he has jaws like those of a lion.
Endowed with that mark, if he lives the life of a householder, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch...
What does he gain when he is a king?
He is invulnerable to any human adversary or enemy.
Being a king, one gains this...
[and so on] ...being a Buddha, what does one gain?
One becomes invulnerable to assault by internal or external enemies and adversaries, through passion.
“Whether by a recluse, a brahmin, a deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world,
nothing can be obtained from one who is a Buddha.
This is the meaning the Blessed One spoke.
Regarding this, it is said:
“He did not engage in idle chatter nor was he arrogant;
his speech and expression were not scattered.”
He dispelled even what was unbeneficial and spoke of what was beneficial and for the happiness of many people. Having done that,
when he passed away from here, he was reborn in heaven.
He experienced the ripening of the fruit of his merit;
having passed away and returned here once more, he attained the supreme,
most excellent, and peerless state of a Universal Monarch.
He becomes a king, difficult to overcome,
a lord of men, a ruler of men, possessed of great majesty;
he becomes equal to the foremost city of the Thirty-three gods.
Like the moon from the most excellent tree of the gods,
he cannot easily be assailed by gandhabbas, asuras, yakkhas, rakkhasas, or even by the devas.
"If he were to exist in such a state, then here would be the directions, the intermediate directions, and the sub-directions.
31–32. The characteristics of the teeth being even and very white.

“Furthermore, monks, in a former birth, a former existence, a former dwelling, having previously been a human being, the Tathāgata abandoned wrong livelihood and made his living by right livelihood. He abstained from cheating with false scales, false weights, and false measures; from bribery, deception, and fraud; and from mutilation, execution, imprisonment, robbery, plunder, and violence.
Because of having performed, accumulated, increased, and expanded that karma, upon the breakup of the body, after death, he was reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.
Thus, there he surpasses other devas in ten respects: by celestial lifespan, by celestial beauty,
by celestial happiness, by celestial glory, by celestial sovereignty, and by celestial forms,
sounds, odors, tastes, and tactile objects.
Passing away from there and returning to this state of existence, he acquires these two marks of a Great Man: his teeth are even and his canine teeth are very white.

Endowed with these marks, if he lives the life of a householder, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch, righteous, a king of Dharma, conqueror of the four quarters, who has established stability in the land and is possessed of the seven treasures.
These are his seven treasures, namely:
The wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh.
Moreover, he has more than a thousand sons who are brave, heroic in form, and crushers of enemy armies.

Having conquered this earth bounded by the ocean—without felling a sword, without using a weapon, but through righteousness alone—he dwells therein, free from all enmity, secure, prosperous, peaceful, auspicious, and without affliction.
Being a king, what does he obtain?

He has a pure retinue; his retinue consists of pure brahmins and householders, citizens and countryfolk, accountants and high officials, military officers, gatekeepers, ministers, counselors, subordinate kings, revenue managers, and princes.
Being a king, this is what he obtains.
But if he goes forth from the home life into homelessness, he becomes an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One who has removed the veil from the world.
Being a Buddha, what does he obtain?
He has a pure retinue; his followers are pure: monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, gods, humans, asuras, nagas, and gandhabbas.
“Being a Buddha, one obtains this.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Regarding this, it is said:
He abandoned wrong livelihood and established a righteous way of life,
pure and in accordance with the Dhamma;
he also cast off what was harmful.
Even though he was dark-skinned, he acted for the happiness of many people.
Having performed deeds with those who are wise, skillful, and virtuous, a man experiences the fruits of happiness in heaven.
Praised as being like the excellent city of the Thirty-three,
he delights there, endowed with pleasure and sport.
Having subsequently obtained a human existence,
Having experienced the ripening of the fruit of well-performed deeds,
one obtains through the remainder a pair of lips that are even,
pure, and very white.
Many fortune-tellers assembled there,
men esteemed for their skill, and they declared:
"He will have a retinue of pure and noble people."
With teeth as even, white, pure,
and beautiful, the king has a large retinue of pure people while he rules over the great earth.
Having overcome the plundering of the countryside,
they practice what is beneficial and brings happiness to many people. Furthermore,
if one goes forth into homelessness, one becomes free from evil.
The ascetic has stilled the dust and removed the veil;
free from distress and weariness,
he beholds this world and the world beyond.
Many householders and renunciants who follow his instruction shake off the impure and censured evil;
for he is indeed surrounded by those who are pure.
“...dispel the stains of the impurity of the Kali age.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Discourse on the Marks is finished; it is the seventh.
